title: The respiratory tract from nose to alveoli
blurb: Trace inhaled air from the nose to the alveoli and say what each structure does along the way.
question: A toddler inhales a small piece of a toy. It slips past the larynx and down the trachea. Which airway is it most likely to lodge in, and what feature of that airway explains it?

teach.body: Formally, the respiratory tract is divided into a conducting zone (nose to the terminal bronchioles), which moves, warms and cleans air but exchanges no gas, and a respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli), where gas exchange happens. In plain English: most of the airway is plumbing that delivers clean, warm, moist air, and only the tiny air sacs at the very end swap oxygen for carbon dioxide.

teach.caption: After the bronchioles come terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts, then the alveoli.
Follow the numbers in order: the pharynx comes before the larynx, and only the alveoli at the end exchange gas.
The thyroid cartilage of the larynx is the Adam's apple. The epiglottis folds over the larynx when you swallow.
Air in the conducting zone (about 150 mL) never reaches the exchange surface: the anatomical dead space.

teach.h: Cartilage fades, muscle and cilia take over
teach.body: The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open at the back where the esophagus lies. Cartilage continues into the bronchi but disappears in the bronchioles, whose walls are smooth muscle. The airway is lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells: the goblet cells make mucus that traps particles, and the cilia sweep it up toward the pharynx. This is the mucociliary escalator.

teach.caption: Both lungs are covered by visceral pleura; parietal pleura lines the chest wall, and pleural fluid between them reduces friction.

teach.body: There are about 300 to 500 million alveoli. Their walls are mostly type I cells, thin simple squamous cells that gases cross easily. Type II cells secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse. Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf debris that got past the mucus. The respiratory membrane that gases diffuse across is the alveolar wall plus the capillary wall.

Jordan, a pre-nursing student volunteering at a pediatric clinic, sees an X-ray of a 3-year-old who inhaled a bead. The bead passed the larynx and trachea and sits in the right main bronchus. Jordan's preceptor explains why: the right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so objects falling straight down the trachea usually go right.

teach.text: Three classic mix-ups: the pharynx is the shared throat while the larynx is the air-only voice box; the epiglottis covers the LARYNX, not the esophagus; and the LEFT lung has 2 lobes (the right has 3). Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, never in the bronchi or ordinary bronchioles.

items: Order: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, primary bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
Conducting zone (to terminal bronchioles) cleans and warms air; no gas exchange.
Respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli) exchanges gas.
Trachea: C-shaped hyaline cartilage; bronchioles: no cartilage, smooth muscle.
Right main bronchus is shorter, wider, more vertical; right lung 3 lobes, left 2.
Type I cells form the exchange surface; type II cells make surfactant.

summary: You can now trace inhaled air from the nasal cavity to the alveoli, separate the conducting zone from the respiratory zone, and explain the job of cartilage, cilia, surfactant and the alveolar cells. You can also explain why aspirated objects usually lodge in the right main bronchus.

A.q: Moving down the airway from the trachea, which is the first level whose walls contain no cartilage?
A.why: Cartilage supports the trachea and all levels of bronchi. It disappears in the bronchioles, whose walls rely on smooth muscle instead.

whyNot.0: Primary (main) bronchi still have cartilage, like the trachea they branch from.
whyNot.1: Tertiary (segmental) bronchi still contain cartilage; it is lost at the next level, the bronchioles.
whyNot.2: Secondary (lobar) bronchi still contain cartilage plates.

A.q: A patient coughs after a sip of water "goes down the wrong way." Which structure failed to fully seal the airway during the swallow?
options: The vocal cords over the trachea
The thyroid cartilage over the glottis
A.why: During swallowing the epiglottis folds over the larynx (the glottis), directing food and drink into the esophagus. If it does not seal in time, liquid enters the larynx and triggers a cough.

whyNot.1: The epiglottis covers the larynx, not the esophagus. Covering the esophagus would block the food route, not the airway.
whyNot.2: The vocal cords sit inside the larynx; sealing the airway entrance during swallowing is the epiglottis's job.
whyNot.3: The thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple) is a fixed part of the larynx wall; it does not fold over anything.

A.q: Compared with the left main bronchus, the right main bronchus is:
A.why: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical, which is why aspirated objects usually lodge on the right.

whyNot.0: The right bronchus is shorter and wider, not longer and narrower.
whyNot.1: It is wider and more vertical; narrower and more horizontal describes the left side better.
whyNot.3: Longer and more horizontal describes the left main bronchus, not the right.

B.q: At which level of the airway does gas exchange first become possible?
B.why: The respiratory zone begins at the respiratory bronchioles, then continues through the alveolar ducts and alveoli. Everything before it is conducting zone.

whyNot.1: Terminal bronchioles are the LAST part of the conducting zone, so no gas exchange happens there.
whyNot.2: Tertiary bronchi are conducting airways with cartilage; they carry air but exchange no gas.
whyNot.3: Primary bronchi are part of the conducting zone and anatomical dead space.

B.q: What is the main function of the surfactant secreted by type II alveolar cells?
options: It raises surface tension so alveoli recoil
It lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open
It traps dust so macrophages can engulf it
It forms the thin layer that gases diffuse across
B.why: Surfactant LOWERS surface tension in the fluid lining the alveoli, which stops them collapsing at the end of each breath.

whyNot.0: Surfactant decreases surface tension; raising it would make alveoli collapse.
whyNot.2: Trapping dust is the job of mucus from goblet cells in the conducting airways.
whyNot.3: The thin diffusion surface is formed by type I cells and the capillary wall, not surfactant.

B.q: Which epithelium lines the trachea and moves mucus up toward the pharynx?
options: Simple squamous, like type I alveolar cells
B.why: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, with goblet cells, lines the conducting airways. Its cilia beat mucus upward: the mucociliary escalator.

whyNot.0: Simple squamous epithelium forms the thin alveolar wall; it has no cilia and does not move mucus.
whyNot.1: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is the skin's surface layer, not an airway lining.
whyNot.2: Simple cuboidal epithelium with microvilli is not the airway lining and does not sweep mucus.

C.q: A 3-year-old aspirates a small bead that passes through the trachea. Where is it most likely to lodge, and why?
options: Right main bronchus: wider, more vertical
Left main bronchus: the left lung is smaller
Right main bronchus: the right lung has 2 lobes
Left main bronchus: shorter and straighter
C.why: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical, so objects falling down the trachea most often enter it.

whyNot.1: Lung size does not steer objects; the shape and angle of the bronchus does, and that favors the right.
whyNot.2: The right lung has 3 lobes, not 2, and lobe count is not what directs an aspirated object.
whyNot.3: The LEFT main bronchus is longer and more angled; the shorter, straighter one is the right.

C.q: Which sequence correctly traces inhaled air from the larynx to the site of gas exchange?
C.why: From the larynx air enters the trachea, then the primary bronchi, which branch down to bronchioles, and finally the alveoli where gas exchange happens.

whyNot.0: Bronchioles come after the bronchi, not before them.
whyNot.1: Alveoli are the end of the pathway, so they cannot come before the bronchioles.
whyNot.2: The pharynx comes BEFORE the larynx, so it cannot follow it on the way down.

C.q: Which statement about the conducting zone is INCORRECT?
options: It warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air
It ends at the terminal bronchioles
It is where most oxygen enters the blood
Its air volume is called dead space
C.why: The conducting zone exchanges no gas at all; oxygen enters the blood in the respiratory zone (mainly the alveoli). So that statement is the incorrect one.

whyNot.0: This is correct: warming, humidifying and filtering air is the conducting zone's job.
whyNot.1: This is correct: the conducting zone runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles.
whyNot.3: This is correct: the roughly 150 mL in the conducting zone is anatomical dead space.

reteach.title: The bronchial tree, upside down
reteach.question: Picture a tree turned upside down inside the chest. Which part of the airway is the trunk, which are the branches, and where are the leaves?

blocks.body: The trachea is the trunk, stiffened by cartilage rings like bark. It splits into two big branches, the primary bronchi, which split again and again. The smallest twigs are the bronchioles, which are soft and muscular with no cartilage. The leaves at the tips are the alveoli, the only place the tree "trades" gases with the blood. Everything from trunk to the last twigs is just the delivery route.

blocks.text: The tree's "trunk" leans: the right main bronchus is the shorter, wider, more vertical branch, so anything dropped down the trunk usually falls to the right.

explain.body: The nasal cavity warms, humidifies and filters air, helped by the nasal conchae. The pharynx (throat) is a passage shared by air and food, in three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx. The larynx (voice box) carries air only; it holds the vocal cords, and the epiglottis covers it during swallowing.

test.q: Which structure is a passageway shared by both air and food?
test.why: The pharynx (throat) carries both air and food before they separate into the larynx and esophagus.

whyNot.1: The larynx carries air only; the epiglottis keeps food out of it.
whyNot.2: The trachea carries air only, down to the bronchi.
whyNot.3: The glottis is the opening of the larynx, which is air only.

explain.body: The trachea is kept open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open at the back next to the esophagus. It divides into right and left primary bronchi, then secondary (lobar) and tertiary (segmental) bronchi. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical.

test.q: The open back of each C-shaped tracheal ring faces which structure?
test.why: The rings are open at the back, where the trachea sits against the esophagus.

whyNot.0: The sternum is in front of the trachea, where the rings are closed.
whyNot.1: The heart lies below and in front, not against the open back of the rings.
whyNot.2: The epiglottis sits above the larynx, not along the trachea's back wall.

explain.body: Conducting zone: nose to the terminal bronchioles. It moves, warms and cleans air but exchanges no gas, so its roughly 150 mL of air is anatomical dead space. Respiratory zone: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli, where gas exchange happens.

test.q: Anatomical dead space is the air that:
options: Remains in the lungs after a maximal exhalation
Fills the conducting zone and is not exchanged
Can be inhaled beyond a normal resting breath
Can be forced out after a normal resting breath
test.why: Anatomical dead space is the air in the conducting airways (about 150 mL), which never reaches an exchange surface.

whyNot.0: Air left after a maximal exhalation is the residual volume, not dead space.
whyNot.2: Extra air inhaled beyond a normal breath is the inspiratory reserve volume.
whyNot.3: Extra air forced out after a normal breath is the expiratory reserve volume.

explain.body: Right lung 3 lobes, left lung 2 (with the cardiac notch). Visceral pleura covers the lungs, parietal pleura lines the chest wall, and pleural fluid reduces friction. Alveolar walls: type I cells (thin, gas exchange), type II cells (surfactant) and macrophages (dust cells).

test.q: Which cells form most of the thin surface across which oxygen diffuses in the alveolus?
test.why: Type I cells are thin simple squamous cells that make up most of the alveolar wall, the gas-exchange surface.

whyNot.0: Type II cells secrete surfactant; they are not the main diffusion surface.
whyNot.1: Macrophages (dust cells) engulf debris; they are not part of the exchange wall.
whyNot.3: Ciliated columnar cells line the conducting airways and sweep mucus; they do not form the alveolar wall.
